terms.gloss: as you like, as you please
terms.grammar: lubet, the older spelling of libet: “as it pleases (you)”
evidence: Ter. And. 310: Age age, ut libet.
Ter. Haut. 738: ut libet. num ego īnstō?
terms.comment: What Terence’s people say when they give in to another’s wish; Traupman’s Estō, ut libet! adds estō to it.

terms.gloss: so be it, as you please
terms.grammar: estō, future imperative of sum, “let it be”; ut lubet (libet), “as it pleases”
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase, made of two classical pieces: estō, granting a point (Plaut., Cic.; see agree), and ut lubet, “as one pleases” (Plaut. Mil. 3.1.111: animō ut lubet, Lewis & Short s.v. bene). Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase.

evidence: Plaut. Trin. 883: Faciam ita ut vīs.
Ter. Haut. 948: Itane vīs? — Ita. — Fīat.

phrases.latin: Vīsne hodiē forīs cēnāre? — Ut libet.
phrases.english: Do you want to eat outside today? — As you wish.

phrases.latin: Tū sī hīc sīs, aliter sentiās. — Age age, ut libet.
phrases.english: If you were in my place, you’d feel differently. — All right, all right, as you wish.

phrases.latin: Sine mē in hāc rē gerere mihi mōrem. — Sinō. Itane vīs? — Ita. — Fīat.
phrases.english: Let me have my way in this. — I’ll let you. Is that what you want? — It is. — So be it.

phrases.latin: Faciam ita ut vīs. Agedum, nōmen tuom prīmum memorā mihi.
phrases.english: I’ll do as you wish. Come on, tell me your name first.

sources: Lewis & Short: sum · Lewis & Short: libet · Lewis & Short: fio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 100, 110, 326, 404.
